solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Animosity engendered by lie involving Republican (8)

indicatorNotes.involving: to involve something is to take it in, so the lie wraps round the letter

blocks.note: a fiction is an untruth
R is the standard abbreviation, placed after the F

annotation.surface: A political row blamed on a falsehood told about a Republican.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a scandal; the parse is just one letter slipped into a synonym for a lie.
annotation.definitionFit: Friction between people is ill feeling or conflict, a close match for animosity.

entries.clue: Young deer of light greyish-brown colour (4)

blocks.note: the name for a deer in its first year
a pale yellowish-brown shade, named after that animal's coat

annotation.surface: A nature-guide description of a young deer's coat.
annotation.walkthrough: The two meanings are really one word in two uses: the colour takes its name from the animal, so the surface reads as a single sensible phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: The colour is named after the young deer's coat, so one word covers both the animal and its shade.

entries.clue: Imprisoned by the enemy, at the last possible moment? (2,3,4,2,4)

blocks.note: read literally: 'the nick' is British slang for prison, and Time is personified as the enemy, so a prisoner sits in Time's jail
the everyday phrase for only just in time

annotation.surface: A war story: captured by the enemy just before rescue could come.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half reads the idiom literally: 'nick' is British slang for a jail, and the enemy is Time personified. The question mark flags the whimsical reading.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done in the nick of time happens at the very last moment it could usefully happen.

entries.clue: Old water board official’s shock over mate in Peckham? (8)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the second

blocks.note: a nasty surprise 'gives you a turn'
'me old cock' is Cockney for mate; Peckham is a working-class district of south London

annotation.surface: A water official gets a fright at a friend's house in south London.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark signals that 'cock' is only 'mate' in London speech. A turncock was the man who turned the water mains on and off.
annotation.definitionFit: A turncock was an employee of a water company who opened and shut the stopcocks on the mains.

entries.clue: Awards divided by old members of orchestra (5)

indicatorNotes.divided by: the awards are split into two parts with the new letter between them

blocks.note: OBEs, the British honour Officer of the Order of the British Empire
O is the abbreviation for old

annotation.surface: Honours shared out among veteran orchestral players.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Members' tempts you towards people; here they are instruments, which count as members of an orchestra's line-up.
annotation.definitionFit: Oboes are woodwind instruments found in every symphony orchestra.

entries.clue: A tax on His Majesty’s neckwear (6)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A VAT placed on CR follows it

blocks.note: Carolus Rex, King Charles's royal cipher
the word itself
value added tax, the British sales tax

annotation.surface: A proposal to tax the King's ties.
annotation.walkthrough: CR stands for Charles Rex, the monarch's cipher; 'His Majesty's' reads as a possessive but just supplies the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A cravat is a scarf-like band of fabric worn around the neck.

entries.clue: Man embracing girl dropping a collector’s item, perhaps (6)

indicatorNotes.embracing: to embrace is to hold in your arms, so the man goes round the girl
indicatorNotes.dropping: the girl lets go of a letter

blocks.note: a man's name
RITA without its A

annotation.surface: A man hugging a girl who fumbles a prized collectable.
annotation.walkthrough: The A in 'dropping a' is both the letter removed and the article of the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A rarity is something rarely found, which is exactly what collectors prize.

entries.clue: Vehicle protector is light, enthralling posh part of Canada (9,6)

indicatorNotes.enthralling: to enthral is to hold captive, so the protector holds the posh letter

blocks.note: a van
a cover protects what is under it
U means upper-class, as in 'U and non-U' speech
the word itself
to light is to alight, to come down and land

annotation.surface: A car cover that is lightweight yet somehow grand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Light' is a verb (a bird lights on a branch), meaning to come down, not an adjective about weight; 'posh' gives the old upper-class label U.
annotation.definitionFit: Vancouver Island is a large island off the Pacific coast of British Columbia, Canada.

entries.clue: Son attempted to keep up record, having wall hangings (10)

indicatorNotes.to keep up: in a down clue, keeping something up means holding it above you, so the record goes on top

blocks.note: to tape is to record
S is the abbreviation for son
tried = attempted

annotation.surface: A son trying to maintain some record, the room decked with hangings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep up a record' reads as maintaining it; in a down clue it means the record sits above S TRIED.
annotation.definitionFit: A tapestried room is hung with tapestries, woven wall hangings.

entries.clue: Emergency food big-billed bird left out for two months? (8)

indicatorNotes.left out: something left out is omitted, so L (left) drops out of the bird
indicatorNotes.for: the two months take the place of, stand in for, the missing L's slot

blocks.note: PELICAN losing L
M is the abbreviation for month, twice

annotation.surface: A pelican set out as emergency rations for a couple of months.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left out' reads as food put out for the bird; it is L being dropped. The question mark marks M for month as a stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: Pemmican is dried pounded meat mixed with fat, a compact ration carried by explorers.

entries.clue: Frightful heat — lower where wild animals drink (5,4)

indicatorNotes.Frightful: something frightful is a terrible mess, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A savannah scene: terrible heat, and the animals lower their heads to drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'lower' look like an instruction to reduce the heat; it is only fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the phrase says what the place is for rather than offering a synonym.

entries.clue: Approach getting former rail union down? (3-2)

indicatorNotes.down?: NUR written down a grid reads RUN when read upwards, which is the answer itself

blocks.note: the National Union of Railwaymen, merged into the RMT in 1990
read the answer as an instruction: RUN, read up, is NUR going down

annotation.surface: An approach that brings a defunct rail union low.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is itself the wordplay: 'RUN up' means write RUN going upwards, giving the NUR that the clue shows going 'down'. The question mark flags this reverse-engineered trick.
annotation.definitionFit: A run-up is the approach, as the period before an event or a bowler's approach to the crease.

entries.clue: German luxury car dealer? Not half (4)

indicatorNotes.Not half: half the word is not there

blocks.note: MERCHANT with its second half, HANT, removed

annotation.surface: A luxury car dealer, and the British exclamation 'Not half!' as enthusiastic agreement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is British slang for 'absolutely', which makes the surface sound like a boast; here it removes half of MERCHANT.
annotation.definitionFit: Merc is informal for a Mercedes-Benz, the German luxury car.

entries.clue: Lavish amount put out round America (9)

indicatorNotes.out: out of order, so the letters of PUT are rearranged

blocks.note: a sum is an amount
PUT rearranged
O is round in shape
the United States

annotation.surface: A generous sum laid out for a tour of the States.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like an instruction to go around America, but it just gives the ring-shaped letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: Sumptuous means splendid and expensive-looking, lavish.

entries.clue: Clock mechanism S African fellows found in east of France (10)

indicatorNotes.found in: the fellows are found inside the French word

blocks.note: est is French for east
the Cape is South Africa's southern tip, as in Cape Town
men = fellows

annotation.surface: South African men turning up in eastern France with a clock part.
annotation.walkthrough: 'East of France' reads as a region (Alsace, say); it means the French word for east, EST.
annotation.definitionFit: The escapement is the part of a clock that releases the gear train one tick at a time.

entries.clue: Wag hiding in school, behind big dipper? (10)

indicatorNotes.hiding in: the wag is concealed inside the school
indicatorNotes.behind: BACK is a synonym, not a position here

blocks.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school
a wag is a joker, a wit
behind = at the back

annotation.surface: A class joker skipping lessons and hiding behind the bike sheds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wag' suggests truancy (to 'wag school' is to skip it), but the word is a noun, a joker. A big dipper is the British name for a roller coaster.
annotation.definitionFit: A switchback is a fairground roller coaster, known in Britain as a big dipper.

entries.clue: Cry of pain in uncovered horse-drawn carriage (8)

indicatorNotes.in: the cry goes inside the word for uncovered

blocks.note: bare = uncovered
the exclamation

annotation.surface: Someone yelps in an open carriage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uncovered' fits a barouche, which had a folding hood, so it looks like part of the definition; it supplies BARE.
annotation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a collapsible top.

entries.clue: Declare a cleric retired (4)

indicatorNotes.retired: to retire is to withdraw, go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the word itself
REV, short for Reverend

annotation.surface: An announcement that a vicar has stepped down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as a vicar's pension; it turns REV round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean asserting something firmly as true.

entries.clue: Inadvertently pick up deliveries, in this place reportedly (8)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is heard, so we want the sound

blocks.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries (balls)
here = in this place

annotation.surface: Someone accidentally collecting parcels meant for this address.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests post; it is cricket, where six balls bowled make an over.
annotation.definitionFit: To overhear is to catch words not meant for you, picking them up by accident.

entries.clue: Article introducing this country’s seabirds (4)

indicatorNotes.introducing: the article comes first and leads into the rest

blocks.note: the indefinite article
UK'S: for a British paper, this country is the UK

annotation.surface: A newspaper feature presenting the nation's seabirds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This country' means the UK, from the point of view of the London-based Times.
annotation.definitionFit: Auks are diving seabirds of northern seas, including puffins and guillemots.

entries.clue: 26 initially managed parts before poetry, making us cross (10)

indicatorNotes.parts: RAN splits the initials in two
indicatorNotes.before: the first part comes ahead of the poetry

blocks.note: 26 across is ELIOT, whose initials are T S
to run a business is to manage it
verse = poetry

annotation.surface: Eliot's poetry, broken into parts, annoys us.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' usually means a first letter; here it means Eliot's initials, T. S. 'Cross' reads as angry but means lying across.
annotation.definitionFit: Transverse means lying or extending across something.

entries.clue: Duck light motor vehicle avoiding a duck? (6)

indicatorNotes.avoiding: the vehicle stays clear of, leaves out, the letter

blocks.note: a scooter is a small, light motorbike
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like the letter O; one O is removed

annotation.surface: A scooter swerving to miss a duck.
annotation.walkthrough: The two ducks differ: the first is the bird defined, the second is cricket's score of nought, shaped like the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: A scoter is a dark sea duck of northern coasts.

entries.clue: Useful doctor left café plugged by university (9)

indicatorNotes.doctor: to doctor is to tamper with, so rearrange the letters
indicatorNotes.plugged by: the jumbled letters take U into a gap

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
U is the abbreviation for university
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A handy GP walks out of a café near the campus.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a noun paired with 'Useful'; it is the verb, meaning to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Effectual means producing the intended result, hence useful.

entries.clue: Lake in which agricultural implement loses power (5)

blocks.note: PLOUGH without P, the abbreviation for power

annotation.surface: A lake where a tractor's plough gives out.
annotation.walkthrough: A lough is the Irish word for a lake, as loch is in Scotland.
annotation.definitionFit: Lough is the Irish term for a lake or sea inlet, as in Lough Neagh.

entries.clue: Report of Aussie native’s ploy (4)

indicatorNotes.Report of: a report is heard, so we want the sound

blocks.note: a roo, a kangaroo, is a native Australian animal

annotation.surface: News of a trick played by an Australian.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Native' suggests a person, but it is the animal: roo is Australian slang for kangaroo.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a cunning trick used to gain an advantage.

entries.clue: Keyed-up broadcasting boss in East Yorkshire originally (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the boss goes inside the initials

blocks.note: the first letters of East and Yorkshire
the Director-General, head of the BBC

annotation.surface: A nervous regional broadcasting chief, a Yorkshire native.
annotation.walkthrough: The BBC's chief is the Director-General, abbreviated DG.
annotation.definitionFit: Edgy means tense and nervous, keyed-up.

entries.clue: One of two writers using revolutionary material (5)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution turns things over, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: toile is a thin linen or cotton fabric
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A pair of authors working with radical subject matter.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is not in the clue: 'material' must first become TOILE. 'Two writers' fits George Eliot and T. S. Eliot.
annotation.definitionFit: Eliot is the surname of both George Eliot and T. S. Eliot, so either writer fits.

entries.clue: Domestic servant’s husband, crazy about one on river (9)

indicatorNotes.about: the crazy word goes round the one
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, placed on the river means following it

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
the Ouse, a river in Yorkshire and another in East Anglia
mad = crazy
the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: A maid's husband going wild about someone on the river.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay, not a possessive.
annotation.definitionFit: A housemaid is a female servant who does housework.

entries.clue: Those folk must hoard gold: that’s the thinking (6)

indicatorNotes.must hoard: to hoard is to keep something inside, so the folk hold the gold

blocks.note: they = those people
or is gold in heraldry

annotation.surface: A cynic's view that the rich will always stockpile gold.
annotation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold, a standard crossword stand-in.
annotation.definitionFit: A theory is a line of thinking, a set of ideas explaining something.

entries.clue: Thus involved with Yard? It’s what Chesterton’s man was (8)

indicatorNotes.involved with: the words are tangled together, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters
anagram fodder, 4 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A detective story: someone mixed up with Scotland Yard.
annotation.walkthrough: G. K. Chesterton's thriller is 'The Man Who Was Thursday', about an undercover detective, which is why Scotland Yard (London's police) suits the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Chesterton's novel is titled 'The Man Who Was Thursday', so Thursday is what his man was.
